concept.name: Market manipulation
concept.definition: Intentional conduct that artificially affects the supply, demand, or price of a security or commodity rather than letting prices reflect genuine market forces — for example, wash trades, matched orders, spoofing, marking the close, or spreading false information to move a price. Section 9 of the Securities Exchange Act and CEA section 4c/6(c) prohibit specific manipulative acts, and Rule 10b-5 reaches manipulative schemes generally.
concept.intuition: It's rigging the scoreboard: instead of predicting where prices will go, the manipulator makes the price move and cashes in on the fake signal everyone else is reacting to.
concept.mechanics: Manipulative schemes work either through trade-based activity (fictitious or dominant trading that moves prints or settlement prices), information-based activity (false rumors or touting), or position-based power (corners and squeezes). Enforcement generally requires proving an artificial price and scienter.
concept.failure_modes: Artificiality is hard to establish when the accused has plausible economic motives, and large legitimate trades inevitably move prices; courts have struggled to draw the line between aggressive trading and manipulation, especially in power and derivatives markets.
concept.misconceptions: Not every price spike, short-selling campaign, or whale order is manipulation — moving the market through genuine, disclosed trading is lawful; manipulation requires deceptive, fictitious, or coercive conduct aimed at creating an artificial price.
concept.example: A trader simultaneously buys a thin stock while placing and cancelling large spoof offers above the market, then posts fake 'breakout' analysis on message boards; the SEC charges a manipulative scheme under Rule 10b-5.
